Conclusion The results of this study highlight grid capacity challenges for airports with expanding electrical loads. The specific challenges in this study were regarding load increases at airport rental car facilities due to the adoption of EVs. However, the resulting solutions could support challenges due to any load increase. If gone unmanaged, these increases in site peak demand would require significant electrical capacity upgrades—$4.2 million for 1.6 MW of additional capacity. While the growing loads from EVs create the challenge of a higher peak demand, the nature of EV charging loads also presents an opportunity. This project developed and tested a site controller specifically to coordinate DER and flexible charging assets to mitigate peak demand concerns and avoid costly upgrades. The simulation results display how simple site management can ensure grid constraints are adhered to and completely avoid infrastructure upgrades. However, these Gold and Platinum results without DER would extend charging times or result in vehicles delivered to customers below the desired SOC. These controls are also able to coordinate with DER assets to further mitigate net peak demand, which would require significantly less investment than the grid upgrades from the uncontrolled scenario—$2.8 million and $1.2 million for Gold and Platinum, respectively. These controls do present a significant improvement in charge session completion compared to uncontrolled and the respective Gold and Platinum non-DER simulations. In addition to the development and simulation of these controls, the team also refined their performance for use in live operations with real-world hardware. This required modifications to the controllers that addressed EVSE hardware capabilities and industry standard communication protocol messages. These updates enabled testing in the CHIL/PHIL test bed to verify system performance at scale. This real-time operation stress test proves the technology could be easily adapted for field demonstrations with equipment available today. While the potential cost savings are significant, and the CHIL/PHIL performance suggests the technology could be deployed in the field, there are some challenges that arose regarding charge session performance. While all of the results above present portions of charge sessions with an SOC deficit, it is important to understand how this is caused. The vehicle itineraries that defined arrival SOC and vehicle dwell period presented many challenges, with a significant portion of the vehicles arriving with less than 30% SOC and many requiring a quick turnaround of less than 30 minutes. While some of these sessions could not be completed under any circumstance due to vehicle charge acceptance curve variability, many others leave very little flexibility for management. Some resolutions to this could include fleet operation revisions that would improve arrival SOC, extended vehicle dwell periods from reservations, or short delivery delays to ensure charge sessions have sufficient time to complete.
